utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I was interrogated twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time you were interrogated, where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That was in a different room, above the canteen that had operated before the war. And I was interrogated in an office upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the second photograph in that bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This may be, then, S15-2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That has been ERN number 00409596.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: You can see the Omarska camp on this picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that how you remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a photograph of a model of the Omarska camp. The model is in the basement of the Tribunal, and it certainly wouldn't fit inside this Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you just point out the buildings that are on that photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This is the white house to which I was brought on the 9th of July. Those are the rooms with the canteen downstairs, while upstairs, there were offices or rooms where inmates were interrogated. Downstairs, on this other side, there were more rooms for inmates. This is the entrance to the canteen. And if you take the stairs, you will find the offices on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the building that you're pointing to, as you look at the photograph, is the littler of the two red buildings, and it's the building to your right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the entrance that you just pointed to was on the left side of that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the larger red building is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Before the war, these were hangars and garages used for the repair of heavy machinery operated in the Omarska mine. So these hangars were used to store the machines, the equipment, and tools needed for repairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when you were taken for interrogation who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during the first interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Some questions were put to me, and I was beaten by those two men. I had nothing to tell them or to confess, but I got beaten nevertheless. I was beaten up there. I was in very bad physical condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of questions were you being asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Some odd questions. I have to apologise, but I have to say this: Those were absolutely stupid, nonsensical questions. And whatever I answered, I would be beaten up. No matter what I said, whether I said yes or no, I would still get beaten. They asked me if I knew Mirza Mujadzic. However, they knew him better than I did. If I said I didn't know him, I would be beaten because I said no. If I said I knew him, I got beaten again, and they would say, in addition: "You were his collaborator, you had planned this together in advance." Briefly, if I said I knew him, it was their version that I was the same as Mirza Mujadzic, and his collaborator. If I said I didn't know him, I was lying. Both ways, I got beaten, no matter what I answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who was Mirza Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Mirza Mujadzic was a doctor before the war, a physician. And I know him as a doctor. He had many patients. And it's true that Mirza Mujadzic was the president of the SDA for the Prijedor municipality. That is common knowledge. Everybody knows that throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, the entire political arena of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entire parliament. Mirza Mujadzic was elected lawfully and was a deputy to the BH parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice the time and that you wanted to stop sitting at 5.00 p.m. today. I have perhaps another 20 minutes worth of questions with the witness. Is it at all possible -- I don't know how long cross-examination would take with this witness, but are we able to indulge the interpreters and yourself to sit any longer today, so that this witness may be able to go home?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I really believe it's better that we can concentrate on the single questions, and when we have time enough for the cross-examination. And therefore I would appreciate when we would stop Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for today and go on the next time with the direct examination and then the cross-examination. Is it correct for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I just hope the witness's employer will indulge us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, let's call it a day for today. And we resume as scheduled, Wednesday morning, 9.00.
